newsitem.title: JAPAN: Russia offers to develop disputed isles with Japan.
newsitem.headline: Russia offers to develop disputed isles with Japan.

text.p: Russia made a formal proposal to Japan on Friday to jointly develop islands at the heart of a long and bitter territorial dispute between the two countries.

Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov made the proposal in talks with former Prime Minister Yasuhiro Nakasone and Taku Yamazaki, policy chief of the ruling Liberal Democratic Party (LDP), LDP officials said.

The row over the islands, called the Southern Kuriles by Russia and Northern Territories by Japan, has prevented the two countries from signing a World War Two treaty and kept bilateral ties in a deep freeze for most of the last 50 years.
"I would like to propose the joint development of the four islands, without damaging the basic positions of both Russia and Japan," LDP officials quoted Primakov as telling Nakasone and Yamazaki.
Primakov was also scheduled to hold talks with Foreign Minister Yukihiko Ikeda and Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto later in the day.
The islands of Etorofu, Kunashiri, Shikotan, and the Habomai group were seized by the advancing Soviet army in the closing days of World War Two.

Russia says the islands are part of its war booty over the entire Kurile chain, stretching from the Kamchatka peninsula to Japan's northernmost Hokkaido islands, promised to them at the Yalta Conference.

But Japan insists the four islands were not a political part of the Kuriles and that Japan was not a party to the Yalta talks. Japan says the four islands have always been part of its territory as far back as 1856 when the Tokugawa Shogunate signed its first treaty with Czarist Russia.
The Soviet government under Stalin heavily favoured the volcanic islands, rich in mineral and fishery resources, offering lucrative wages to potential Russian immigrants.

In 1956 when the two countries normalised ties, the Kremlin offered to hand back two of the islands to Japan upon conclusion of a World War Two peace treaty and then discuss the future of the other two after that.
But when Japan signed the 1960 U.S.-Japan Security Treaty, Moscow repudiated the 1956 pledge and until the late 1980s insisted that the territorial issue did not exist at all.
A new phase came with Russian President Boris Yeltsin's visit to Tokyo in 1993, when he promised to address the territorial dispute based on "law and justice".

The sparsely populated islands have now become a backwater for Russia, suffering from chronic economic shortages. Politically, however, Yeltsin is unable to concede very much on territorial disputes anywhere because of fears of a nationalistic backlash.

The islands are also the scene of frequent clashes over fishing rights. Japanese fishing boats have often ventured into what Russia claims as its own waters, resulting in many shooting incidents by border patrols.
